nodes.text: Dabney House

He thinks on this one, goes to the easy place and there is a sudden narrative skip ahead, two hours later, having landed at LAX, catching a shuttle to Caltech, Janessa brings Andy to sit under a mural at Dabney House entitled The Birth of God.
It depicts an old man in a striped shirt and overalls.
The first thing they do, sit here and talk catch-up. Cat soup. Janessa brings out lunch, a few steamed dumplings and hoisin sauce.
They eat in relative silence.

The air is new and so fresh and Andy does not know quite what to make of any of this not so subtle change of scenery. Texas a toxic death cloud when he left. A greenhouse of suffocating summer heat and sweat in his eyes like tears.
The crisp bright newness of California makes him sneeze in fits.

The courtyard is quiet, few people pass in and under courtyard archways, look out the inner windows music playing from somewhere high up carried on tiny speakers and mp3 computer terminals that anyone at anytime can access and change the general ambiance of the much bigger central place with whatever selection they want whenever they want.
It's a commune he realizes and he sees why his sister likes this place so damn much. Why he sees so little of her because she's so in love with this.
Somewhere up there a song cuts off mid-chorus and something else starts in its place.
Palm trees and dead fronds fallen at the base ebb in the strong mid-afternoon breeze.

Old adolescent scraggly kittens play a bit too mean and aggressive, Janessa reminds Andy she gets paid by the school to volunteer at the SPCA and says she'll have to take the kittens away soon as soon as they've stopped being so darn cute.

Janessa tells Andy a story about her freshman year, about the games they played when she first got there, not so much a game as a series of games, extreme challenges thought out rendered executed with fine honed Caltech nerd precision.
The stacks.
Know where the term comes from?
Programming, I think. I remember that from my computer science days. A stack.
A series of 8 or something. A series of storage things. God, this is the reason I'm not a computer scientist.
"Sorta," she says and goes into a bit more detail about the stacks themselves.

Janessa was frosh, she was initiate. Early on in the year every older student gangs up to challenge frosh, to bring them into the Caltech fold proper. One year, Janessa says, they threw frosh into the back of the van, made them drink electric Kool-Aid and the little bastards Fear and Loathed all the way to Vegas.
Andy laughs. She continues. When they got there, there was a whole series of tests and games they had to pass.
Math problems, logic problems, strange shit thrown into just confound the poor babies.
So — what crazy shit did you have to participate in your freshman year?
Janessa smiles, "I haven't told you about this?"
Andy shakes his head, smiles.
Video games, that was our theme.

It began with several freshmen being concreted into their rooms overnight unaware. It was up to all the rest to free their imprisoned comrades first off. Upperclassmen made it clear the kids on the inside had half a clue and the kids outside the missing piece.
There were many different solutions to the primary cask of amontillado scenario. One involved a jackhammer, another a fireman air cushion to jump into for the bravest soul among froshkind.
The next discovery was a set of clues entombed in the bathrooms of Dabney Hall. They were told not to try and budge the front doors. Instead they were told to go to higher ground.

Frosh found new holes in the floor where no holes were before. Peering into the holes they saw dark water. The older students had sealed and flooded the bathrooms overnight, and now the frosh had to swim down into the bathrooms and look for uneasy answers.
There were chains and locks and heavy things at the bottom. They had to find keys in the dark before they could get at the objects themselves.
What were they?
Metal puzzle pieces the industrial art kids had welded, three dimensional abstract. They had to assemble them under water under eight feet of water.
And then what?
The sculpture spelled out a word, '8-bit'.
Huh. Old-school video game, Nintendo was 8-bit for sure.

We went down to the game room which is where you'll be sleeping and hooked up was an old nintendo. Somehow the older kids had made their own ROMS, their own video games, and we had to play through them. They had me play the Zelda knock-off since my last name was Link.
It was a breeze, my clue was just one part of the greater whole. When everyone finished up their respective games we went on to the next stack challenge. It just got more insane as it went along.
Andy and Janessa both finish up their buns and throw the trash away. The stack story ends and Janessa uses the natural pause to show Andy around campus, they walk just about everywhere.
Janessa carries a bottle of water with her everywhere she goes because she's big on hydration.
Where are all your friends?
They only come out at night. They're all still asleep or they're at their summer jobs or internships. I'm treating you to dinner tonight.
Rather, Jessie and Spencer are, since Spencer has a car.

Janessa gets an idea and drags Andy to the side of the building. Under a tarp is a couch only it has been lifted off the ground and underneath are two large sets of wheels, an engine and a make-shift handlebar steering wheel, all welded fitted into awkward looking monstrosity.
Behold the couchmobile. A bunch of us are still working on it but it should be up and running before you leave. It's the only way to get around campus.
"You guys made this," Andy says. He sits on the machine and looks out at the overgrown ivy wall that separates the campus from the greater city of Pasadena.
Comfy son of a bitch.
